chunk_findings.detail: The capture path unconditionally uses a process-wide `RUSAGE_CHILDREN` before/after delta even on Linux/macOS where `wait4` is available, because it calls `R.measure(None, before)` instead of metering the child directly. `RUSAGE_CHILDREN` is global to the whole ddflow process, so any child reaped by another thread or by unrelated code during the capture is charged to this command. For example, if thread A calls `capture(["python", "-c", "print(1)"])` while thread B runs and reaps a CPU-heavy child, thread A’s `Captured.resources.cpu_user_s` can include thread B’s child. The same snapshot is also invalid for peak RSS: `RUSAGE_CHILDREN.ru_maxrss` is a monotonic high-water mark over all waited-for children, not a per-interval peak. After one child peaks at 500 MB, a later command that peaks at 10 MB will yield a maxrss delta of 0 (or 500 MB if the code uses the after value), so `maxrss_kb` is not the command’s peak RSS.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/proc.py:capture

chunk_findings.detail: The new metering is attached to the direct child created by `popen(command, cls=MeteredPopen, shell=True, ...)`, which is the shell process, not the full gate-command tree. For an input such as `run_shell("sleep 5 | cat")`, or any command that spawns helper processes, the metered PID is `/bin/sh`; `wait4` on that PID returns only the shell’s own resources (often near zero), and the descendants’ CPU, RSS, and block I/O are not included. Starting the command in a process group does not make kernel `rusage` aggregate a process tree, so the resulting `cpu_user_s`, `maxrss_kb`, and I/O fields can be materially wrong for the actual gate command.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/proc.py:_run_shell

chunk_findings.detail: In the timeout path, `_note_cost` is called only after `kill_group(p)` and `_drain(p)`, and only when `p.returncode is not None`. For a standard `subprocess.Popen`, `returncode` becomes non-`None` only after `Popen.wait()`/`poll()` has already reaped the child via `os.waitpid`; once that has happened, `os.wait4()` cannot retrieve that child's rusage (it will fail with `ChildProcessError`). If `_drain` does not reap the child, `p.returncode` remains `None` and `_note_cost` silently records nothing. Thus a timed-out gate command cannot produce the intended per-child `wait4` evidence: either no `Resources` are appended, or the implementation must fall back to the process-wide `RUSAGE_CHILDREN` before/after delta. That delta is not per-child attribution: for example, if another ddflow child is running or is waited for during the interval, its CPU/RSS can be charged to the timed-out command; if the timed-out child was not properly reaped by this process, its usage can be omitted entirely. This violates the stated requirement that `wait4` provide the child's own user/system CPU, maxrss, and block I/O, with delta only when `wait4` is genuinely unusable.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/proc.py:_note_cost

chunk_findings.detail: The fake rusage tests hard-code Linux units but do not control the platform. On macOS (`sys.platform == "darwin"`), `ru_maxrss` is bytes and the change is required to normalise it to KB; `_ru()` sets `ru_maxrss=2048`, so a compliant `R.from_rusage(_ru())` should produce `maxrss_kb == 2`, not `2048`. The same assumption breaks `test_measure_prefers_wait4_then_delta_then_unavailable`, where fake `ru_maxrss=4096` becomes 4 KB on macOS, so the assertion `d.maxrss_kb == 4096` fails. These tests will fail on a supported macOS run unless they monkeypatch the platform or use platform-appropriate raw values.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_resource_capture.py:test_from_rusage_fake_gives_the_evidence_fields

chunk_findings.detail: The real-child tests interpolate `sys.executable` directly into a shell string without quoting. If the Python executable path contains spaces (for example `[REDACTED:path] Doe/.venv/bin/python`), the command becomes `[REDACTED:path] Doe/.venv/bin/python -c '...'`, which the shell parses as program `[REDACTED:path]` with extra arguments. The child never starts, `r.ok` is false, and the resource-capture tests fail. The tests should quote `sys.executable` (e.g. `shlex.quote`).
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_resource_capture.py:test_real_child_that_allocates_and_burns_cpu_is_measured

chunk_findings.detail: This test asserts that a normal POSIX `P.capture([sys.executable, "-c", "print(1)"], timeout=20)` reports `resources_source == "delta"`. The stated intent requires `capture` to use per-child `wait4` when it is usable and to fall back to a delta only when `wait4` is not usable. On normal Linux/macOS, a compliant `capture` should therefore report `wait4`; this test either fails against the correct implementation or locks in an implementation that never uses `wait4` for capture.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_resource_capture.py:test_capture_reports_an_approximate_delta

chunk_findings.detail: The burn fixture allocates 150 MB and the real-child test requires peak RSS of at least 140 MB. In a memory-constrained but otherwise supported environment (for example a container with a 128 MB cgroup limit, or several pytest-xdist workers sharing a small container), `bytearray(150 * 1024 * 1024)` raises `MemoryError`, `r.ok` becomes false, and the resource-capture tests fail. The allocation size should be adaptive, configurable, or skipped when the process cannot allocate enough memory.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_resource_capture.py:_BURN

chunk_findings.detail: `resource.RUSAGE_CHILDREN.ru_maxrss` is a high-water mark over all previously reaped children in the process, not a per-child delta. The code sets `ru_maxrss = after.ru_maxrss`, so when wait4 is unusable and an earlier child had a larger peak RSS, that previous child’s peak is attributed to the current command. Example: child A ran with a 1 GiB peak and was waited normally; later child B is run with SIGCHLD ignored, so wait4 fails. The before and after `children_snapshot()` values both still carry A’s 1 GiB high-water mark, and B’s evidence records `maxrss_kb=1048576` even if B used 2 MiB. Because the field is recorded as `maxrss_kb` while only the imperfect `resources_source=delta` hints it may be approximate, this is wrong per-command peak RSS data.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/resources.py:110 `_delta`

chunk_findings.detail: The assertion `res.cpu_user_s + res.cpu_sys_s >= 0.35` is wrong for the wait4 path. `P.run_shell(f"{sys.executable} -c '{_BURN}' & wait")` executes `/bin/sh -c 'python -c <burn> & wait'`; the direct child of `ddflow` is the shell, and the Python process that burns 0.4s is a grandchild. `wait4` on the direct shell child reports only the shell's own `ru_utime`/`ru_stime` (a few milliseconds), not the background child's CPU. This same test file relies on `P.run_shell` reaping the shell via `P.MeteredPopen` (see line 117), so normal execution of this input will produce far below 0.35 and the test fails.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_resource_capture.py:91

chunk_findings.detail: This test no longer checks that `maxrss_kb` is per-command. The previous version asserted that a cheap command run after a heavy one did not inherit the heavy command's peak RSS (`again.maxrss_kb < 50 * 1024`); the diff replaced that with only a CPU comparison. If `resources.py`’s wait4 path were changed to return a process-wide high-water `maxrss_kb` (e.g. from `RUSAGE_CHILDREN` or a cached maximum), the sequence `true`, heavy burn, `true` would still pass: `cheap.source == again.source == "wait4"` and `again.cpu < heavy.cpu/2` can both be true while `again.maxrss_kb` is incorrectly the heavy child’s peak. Since per-command peak RSS is a core requirement of this change, removing the only regression assertion for non-running-total maxrss lets a wrong implementation pass.

Either the production code discards an available metric on a supported platform, or the test fails on macOS when `from_rusage` forwards those fields. A child that does no block I/O should record a legitimate `0`, not appear as “unknown”.

chunk_findings.detail: This path records per-command cost from a `RUSAGE_CHILDREN` before/after delta. `ru_maxrss` is a high-water mark over all children already waited for, not a cumulative counter, so a before/after delta cannot recover the newly run child’s peak RSS. For example, if an earlier ddflow child peaked at 100 MB and then this capture path runs a child that peaks at 1 MB, the after snapshot still reports the prior 100 MB high-water mark; subtracting yields 0 KB (or reporting the after value yields 100 MB), so the evidence misreports `maxrss_kb` for a command that actually allocated memory. The delta source should mark peak RSS unavailable rather than emit a per-command `maxrss_kb` that is structurally wrong.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/proc.py:run_shell capture path (`resources=R.measure(None, before)`)

chunk_findings.detail: `p.communicate(timeout=wait)` is a standard Unix `subprocess.Popen` call: when it returns normally it has already called `Popen.wait()` and reaped the child. `_note_cost` is then called after that reap, so the kernel can no longer supply per-child `wait4` rusage for `p.pid`; an `os.wait4(p.pid, 0)` attempt after a normal `communicate()` return gets `ECHILD`. Thus, for a gate command that exits normally, the new code cannot produce the intended `resources_source="wait4"` per-command CPU/RSS/IO evidence. If `R.measure` falls back to a `RUSAGE_CHILDREN` delta, the values are approximate over every child reaped since `before` (for example the watcher or another concurrent child), not the gate command’s own usage. The rusage must be captured before the child is reaped, or stored by the code that reaps it, rather than after standard `communicate()` has already reaped it.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/proc.py:436 (`_note_cost` call after `p.communicate`)

chunk_findings.detail: The change introduces direct OS resource capture in `ddflow/infra/resources.py` and wires the concrete result object into `cmdrunner._finish` and `gates.runner._cost_evidence`, rather than exposing kernel child rusage/wait4 through a port in `ddflow/adapters`. Kernel rusage/wait4 is an external dependency outside the process (the guidance explicitly lists subprocess tools, clocks, and environment as things that must be ported), so any fake, swap, or unsupported-platform test has to reach into the concrete `infra.resources` module and shared service files instead of using a single adapter port; this violates [r-adapters].
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/resources.py (new) / ddflow/services/cmdrunner.py:185

chunk_findings.detail: This test runs `P.run_shell(f"{_PY} -c '{_BURN}' & wait")` and requires `cpu_user_s + cpu_sys_s >= 0.35`. On POSIX, the runner’s direct child is the shell; the Python process is a grandchild and is reaped by the shell’s `wait`. `wait4()` returns rusage only for the direct child being waited on, and `getrusage(RUSAGE_CHILDREN)` reports only direct children that the calling process has waited for. Starting the shell in a new process group does not make the runner the parent of the background Python process. Therefore on Linux/macOS the runner will normally see the shell’s tiny CPU time, not the Python burn’s ~0.4s, so the assertion fails unless tree attribution is done by some non-stdlib mechanism not described in the change.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_resource_capture.py:test_a_process_tree_is_attributed_to_the_shell_line

chunk_findings.detail: This test asserts that a successful `P.capture([sys.executable, "-c", "print(1)"])` reports `resources_source == "delta"`. The stated intent is that capture uses per-child `wait4` and falls back to a before/after `RUSAGE_CHILDREN` delta only when `wait4` is not usable. For the direct child in this test, `wait4` is usable on POSIX (the same `MeteredPopen`/`wait4` path used by `run_shell` can capture pipes). Thus the test either rejects a conforming `wait4` implementation or encodes that the shipped `capture` uses approximate deltas even when `wait4` is available, violating the “fallback only when wait4 is not usable” requirement.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_resource_capture.py:test_capture_reports_an_approximate_delta

chunk_findings.detail: `run_shell` passes a mutable `cost` list into `run(...)` and then derives `ShellResult.resources` from `cost[0]`, but the `run` implementation never mutates that list. The diff adds the `cost` parameter and a `before = R.children_snapshot()` call, then starts `MeteredPopen`, but adds no `R.measure(...)` result and no `cost.append(...)`/`cost[0] = ...` after the child is waited. As a result `cost` remains empty for success and timeout alike, so every command executed via `run_shell` returns `resources=None`. This defeats the intended wait4 resource capture for `run_shell`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/proc.py:416 (`run` / `run_shell` cost list)

chunk_findings.detail: The change adds a new external resource-measurement dependency under `ddflow/infra` and consumes it directly from `ddflow/infra/proc.py`. The project rule requires every external dependency to go through a port in `ddflow/adapters`, but no `ddflow/adapters` port is added in this manifest; the new `resources` module is not an adapter port. This violates [r-adapters] and prevents the single-place swap/fake that the rule calls for.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/proc.py:29 / ddflow/infra/resources.py [r-adapters]

chunk_findings.detail: After `p.communicate()` returns on the normal success path, the child process has already been reaped by `subprocess` (`communicate` calls `self.wait()` after reading EOF, so `p.returncode` is non-None). On Linux/macOS, `os.wait4(p.pid)` then raises `ChildProcessError` (ECHILD); there is no per-child rusage left to collect. Example: `run_shell(["sh","-c","python -c 'range(10**6)'"], cost=[])` — the command completes, `_note_cost(cost, p, before)` calls `R.measure` after the pid is gone, so the advertised wait4 per-child capture cannot happen; it either propagates the ECHILD error instead of returning a `CompletedProcess` or silently falls back to the approximate `RUSAGE_CHILDREN` delta, never recording the child's own cpu/maxrss/io. The call must happen before any `wait()`/`communicate()` reap, or the run loop must perform its own read/select loop and call `os.wait4` itself.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/proc.py:_note_cost

chunk_findings.detail: The test runs `P.run_shell(f"{_PY} -c '{_BURN}' & wait")` and asserts the shell line’s resources show `cpu_user_s + cpu_sys_s >= 0.35`. On POSIX with a `shell=True`-style `run_shell`, the direct child is `/bin/sh -c "python ... & wait"`; that shell spends almost no CPU and the Python background child is a descendant, not the direct child. `wait4` on the shell returns only the shell’s own rusage, and putting the shell in its own process group does not make `wait4` aggregate descendants. The assertion will fail (or the capture would have to misreport the shell’s own usage as the child’s).
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_resource_capture.py::test_a_process_tree_is_attributed_to_the_shell_line

chunk_findings.detail: The capture path unconditionally uses a process-wide `RUSAGE_CHILDREN` before/after delta even on Linux/macOS where `wait4` is available, because it calls `R.measure(None, before)` instead of metering the child directly. `RUSAGE_CHILDREN` is global to the whole ddflow process, so any child reaped by another thread or by unrelated code during the capture is charged to this command. For example, if thread A calls `capture(["python", "-c", "print(1)"])` while thread B runs and reaps a CPU-heavy child, thread A’s `Captured.resources.cpu_user_s` can include thread B’s child. The same snapshot is also invalid for peak RSS: `RUSAGE_CHILDREN.ru_maxrss` is a monotonic high-water mark over all waited-for children, not a per-interval peak. After one child peaks at 500 MB, a later command that peaks at 10 MB will yield a maxrss delta of 0 (or 500 MB if the code uses the after value), so `maxrss_kb` is not the command’s peak RSS.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/proc.py:capture

chunk_findings.detail: The new metering is attached to the direct child created by `popen(command, cls=MeteredPopen, shell=True, ...)`, which is the shell process, not the full gate-command tree. For an input such as `run_shell("sleep 5 | cat")`, or any command that spawns helper processes, the metered PID is `/bin/sh`; `wait4` on that PID returns only the shell’s own resources (often near zero), and the descendants’ CPU, RSS, and block I/O are not included. Starting the command in a process group does not make kernel `rusage` aggregate a process tree, so the resulting `cpu_user_s`, `maxrss_kb`, and I/O fields can be materially wrong for the actual gate command.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/proc.py:_run_shell

chunk_findings.detail: In the timeout path, `_note_cost` is called only after `kill_group(p)` and `_drain(p)`, and only when `p.returncode is not None`. For a standard `subprocess.Popen`, `returncode` becomes non-`None` only after `Popen.wait()`/`poll()` has already reaped the child via `os.waitpid`; once that has happened, `os.wait4()` cannot retrieve that child's rusage (it will fail with `ChildProcessError`). If `_drain` does not reap the child, `p.returncode` remains `None` and `_note_cost` silently records nothing. Thus a timed-out gate command cannot produce the intended per-child `wait4` evidence: either no `Resources` are appended, or the implementation must fall back to the process-wide `RUSAGE_CHILDREN` before/after delta. That delta is not per-child attribution: for example, if another ddflow child is running or is waited for during the interval, its CPU/RSS can be charged to the timed-out command; if the timed-out child was not properly reaped by this process, its usage can be omitted entirely. This violates the stated requirement that `wait4` provide the child's own user/system CPU, maxrss, and block I/O, with delta only when `wait4` is genuinely unusable.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/proc.py:_note_cost

chunk_findings.detail: The fake rusage tests hard-code Linux units but do not control the platform. On macOS (`sys.platform == "darwin"`), `ru_maxrss` is bytes and the change is required to normalise it to KB; `_ru()` sets `ru_maxrss=2048`, so a compliant `R.from_rusage(_ru())` should produce `maxrss_kb == 2`, not `2048`. The same assumption breaks `test_measure_prefers_wait4_then_delta_then_unavailable`, where fake `ru_maxrss=4096` becomes 4 KB on macOS, so the assertion `d.maxrss_kb == 4096` fails. These tests will fail on a supported macOS run unless they monkeypatch the platform or use platform-appropriate raw values.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_resource_capture.py:test_from_rusage_fake_gives_the_evidence_fields

chunk_findings.detail: The real-child tests interpolate `sys.executable` directly into a shell string without quoting. If the Python executable path contains spaces (for example `[REDACTED:path] Doe/.venv/bin/python`), the command becomes `[REDACTED:path] Doe/.venv/bin/python -c '...'`, which the shell parses as program `[REDACTED:path]` with extra arguments. The child never starts, `r.ok` is false, and the resource-capture tests fail. The tests should quote `sys.executable` (e.g. `shlex.quote`).
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_resource_capture.py:test_real_child_that_allocates_and_burns_cpu_is_measured

chunk_findings.detail: This test asserts that a normal POSIX `P.capture([sys.executable, "-c", "print(1)"], timeout=20)` reports `resources_source == "delta"`. The stated intent requires `capture` to use per-child `wait4` when it is usable and to fall back to a delta only when `wait4` is not usable. On normal Linux/macOS, a compliant `capture` should therefore report `wait4`; this test either fails against the correct implementation or locks in an implementation that never uses `wait4` for capture.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_resource_capture.py:test_capture_reports_an_approximate_delta

chunk_findings.detail: The burn fixture allocates 150 MB and the real-child test requires peak RSS of at least 140 MB. In a memory-constrained but otherwise supported environment (for example a container with a 128 MB cgroup limit, or several pytest-xdist workers sharing a small container), `bytearray(150 * 1024 * 1024)` raises `MemoryError`, `r.ok` becomes false, and the resource-capture tests fail. The allocation size should be adaptive, configurable, or skipped when the process cannot allocate enough memory.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_resource_capture.py:_BURN

chunk_findings.detail: `resource.RUSAGE_CHILDREN.ru_maxrss` is a high-water mark over all previously reaped children in the process, not a per-child delta. The code sets `ru_maxrss = after.ru_maxrss`, so when wait4 is unusable and an earlier child had a larger peak RSS, that previous child’s peak is attributed to the current command. Example: child A ran with a 1 GiB peak and was waited normally; later child B is run with SIGCHLD ignored, so wait4 fails. The before and after `children_snapshot()` values both still carry A’s 1 GiB high-water mark, and B’s evidence records `maxrss_kb=1048576` even if B used 2 MiB. Because the field is recorded as `maxrss_kb` while only the imperfect `resources_source=delta` hints it may be approximate, this is wrong per-command peak RSS data.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/resources.py:110 `_delta`

chunk_findings.detail: The assertion `res.cpu_user_s + res.cpu_sys_s >= 0.35` is wrong for the wait4 path. `P.run_shell(f"{sys.executable} -c '{_BURN}' & wait")` executes `/bin/sh -c 'python -c <burn> & wait'`; the direct child of `ddflow` is the shell, and the Python process that burns 0.4s is a grandchild. `wait4` on the direct shell child reports only the shell's own `ru_utime`/`ru_stime` (a few milliseconds), not the background child's CPU. This same test file relies on `P.run_shell` reaping the shell via `P.MeteredPopen` (see line 117), so normal execution of this input will produce far below 0.35 and the test fails.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_resource_capture.py:91

chunk_findings.detail: This test no longer checks that `maxrss_kb` is per-command. The previous version asserted that a cheap command run after a heavy one did not inherit the heavy command's peak RSS (`again.maxrss_kb < 50 * 1024`); the diff replaced that with only a CPU comparison. If `resources.py`’s wait4 path were changed to return a process-wide high-water `maxrss_kb` (e.g. from `RUSAGE_CHILDREN` or a cached maximum), the sequence `true`, heavy burn, `true` would still pass: `cheap.source == again.source == "wait4"` and `again.cpu < heavy.cpu/2` can both be true while `again.maxrss_kb` is incorrectly the heavy child’s peak. Since per-command peak RSS is a core requirement of this change, removing the only regression assertion for non-running-total maxrss lets a wrong implementation pass.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_resource_capture.py:test_each_command_gets_its_own_numbers_not_a_running_total

chunk_findings.detail: This test locks in that `R.from_rusage(..., platform="darwin")` returns `(None, None)` for `ru_inblock=0`/`ru_oublock=0`, but Darwin’s rusage struct does expose `ru_inblock` and `ru_oublock`. Either the production code discards an available metric on a supported platform, or the test fails on macOS when `from_rusage` forwards those fields. A child that does no block I/O should record a legitimate `0`, not appear as “unknown”.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_resource_capture.py:test_macos_block_io_is_unknown_not_zero

chunk_findings.detail: The new `except subprocess.TimeoutExpired` path meters the timed-out capture with `R.measure(None, before)`, i.e. a process-wide `RUSAGE_CHILDREN` before/after delta, not the timed-out child's own `wait4` rusage. Because `RUSAGE_CHILDREN` accumulates every child reaped by the ddflow process, a concurrent reap is charged to this command: if thread A calls `capture([sys.executable, "-c", "import time; time.sleep(30)"], timeout=0.3)` and thread B starts and reaps a CPU-heavy child while A is waiting, A's returned `Resources.cpu_user_s` includes B's CPU although the sleep command used almost none. This is the previously confirmed capture-delta misattribution still present in the new timeout path.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/proc.py:capture timeout except

chunk_findings.detail: The burn fixture now allocates 200 MB (`bytearray(200 * 1024 * 1024)`) and the real-child tests require peak RSS of at least 180 MB, regressing the earlier reduction to 100 MB/90 MB. In a supported but memory-constrained CI environment (for example a 128 MB cgroup limit, or several pytest-xdist workers each trying to allocate 200 MB), the child raises `MemoryError`, so `P.run_shell(...).resources` is not usable and `test_a_real_child_that_allocates_and_burns_cpu_is_measured` plus the maxrss assertions in `test_each_command_gets_its_own_numbers_not_a_running_total` fail.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_resource_capture.py:_BURN

chunk_findings.detail: This path records per-command cost from a `RUSAGE_CHILDREN` before/after delta. `ru_maxrss` is a high-water mark over all children already waited for, not a cumulative counter, so a before/after delta cannot recover the newly run child’s peak RSS. For example, if an earlier ddflow child peaked at 100 MB and then this capture path runs a child that peaks at 1 MB, the after snapshot still reports the prior 100 MB high-water mark; subtracting yields 0 KB (or reporting the after value yields 100 MB), so the evidence misreports `maxrss_kb` for a command that actually allocated memory. The delta source should mark peak RSS unavailable rather than emit a per-command `maxrss_kb` that is structurally wrong.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/proc.py:run_shell capture path (`resources=R.measure(None, before)`)

chunk_findings.detail: `p.communicate(timeout=wait)` is a standard Unix `subprocess.Popen` call: when it returns normally it has already called `Popen.wait()` and reaped the child. `_note_cost` is then called after that reap, so the kernel can no longer supply per-child `wait4` rusage for `p.pid`; an `os.wait4(p.pid, 0)` attempt after a normal `communicate()` return gets `ECHILD`. Thus, for a gate command that exits normally, the new code cannot produce the intended `resources_source="wait4"` per-command CPU/RSS/IO evidence. If `R.measure` falls back to a `RUSAGE_CHILDREN` delta, the values are approximate over every child reaped since `before` (for example the watcher or another concurrent child), not the gate command’s own usage. The rusage must be captured before the child is reaped, or stored by the code that reaps it, rather than after standard `communicate()` has already reaped it.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/proc.py:436 (`_note_cost` call after `p.communicate`)

chunk_findings.detail: The change introduces direct OS resource capture in `ddflow/infra/resources.py` and wires the concrete result object into `cmdrunner._finish` and `gates.runner._cost_evidence`, rather than exposing kernel child rusage/wait4 through a port in `ddflow/adapters`. Kernel rusage/wait4 is an external dependency outside the process (the guidance explicitly lists subprocess tools, clocks, and environment as things that must be ported), so any fake, swap, or unsupported-platform test has to reach into the concrete `infra.resources` module and shared service files instead of using a single adapter port; this violates [r-adapters].
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/resources.py (new) / ddflow/services/cmdrunner.py:185

chunk_findings.detail: This test runs `P.run_shell(f"{_PY} -c '{_BURN}' & wait")` and requires `cpu_user_s + cpu_sys_s >= 0.35`. On POSIX, the runner’s direct child is the shell; the Python process is a grandchild and is reaped by the shell’s `wait`. `wait4()` returns rusage only for the direct child being waited on, and `getrusage(RUSAGE_CHILDREN)` reports only direct children that the calling process has waited for. Starting the shell in a new process group does not make the runner the parent of the background Python process. Therefore on Linux/macOS the runner will normally see the shell’s tiny CPU time, not the Python burn’s ~0.4s, so the assertion fails unless tree attribution is done by some non-stdlib mechanism not described in the change.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_resource_capture.py:test_a_process_tree_is_attributed_to_the_shell_line

chunk_findings.detail: This test asserts that a successful `P.capture([sys.executable, "-c", "print(1)"])` reports `resources_source == "delta"`. The stated intent is that capture uses per-child `wait4` and falls back to a before/after `RUSAGE_CHILDREN` delta only when `wait4` is not usable. For the direct child in this test, `wait4` is usable on POSIX (the same `MeteredPopen`/`wait4` path used by `run_shell` can capture pipes). Thus the test either rejects a conforming `wait4` implementation or encodes that the shipped `capture` uses approximate deltas even when `wait4` is available, violating the “fallback only when wait4 is not usable” requirement.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_resource_capture.py:test_capture_reports_an_approximate_delta

chunk_findings.detail: `run_shell` passes a mutable `cost` list into `run(...)` and then derives `ShellResult.resources` from `cost[0]`, but the `run` implementation never mutates that list. The diff adds the `cost` parameter and a `before = R.children_snapshot()` call, then starts `MeteredPopen`, but adds no `R.measure(...)` result and no `cost.append(...)`/`cost[0] = ...` after the child is waited. As a result `cost` remains empty for success and timeout alike, so every command executed via `run_shell` returns `resources=None`. This defeats the intended wait4 resource capture for `run_shell`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/proc.py:416 (`run` / `run_shell` cost list)

chunk_findings.detail: The change adds a new external resource-measurement dependency under `ddflow/infra` and consumes it directly from `ddflow/infra/proc.py`. The project rule requires every external dependency to go through a port in `ddflow/adapters`, but no `ddflow/adapters` port is added in this manifest; the new `resources` module is not an adapter port. This violates [r-adapters] and prevents the single-place swap/fake that the rule calls for.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/proc.py:29 / ddflow/infra/resources.py [r-adapters]

chunk_findings.detail: After `p.communicate()` returns on the normal success path, the child process has already been reaped by `subprocess` (`communicate` calls `self.wait()` after reading EOF, so `p.returncode` is non-None). On Linux/macOS, `os.wait4(p.pid)` then raises `ChildProcessError` (ECHILD); there is no per-child rusage left to collect. Example: `run_shell(["sh","-c","python -c 'range(10**6)'"], cost=[])` — the command completes, `_note_cost(cost, p, before)` calls `R.measure` after the pid is gone, so the advertised wait4 per-child capture cannot happen; it either propagates the ECHILD error instead of returning a `CompletedProcess` or silently falls back to the approximate `RUSAGE_CHILDREN` delta, never recording the child's own cpu/maxrss/io. The call must happen before any `wait()`/`communicate()` reap, or the run loop must perform its own read/select loop and call `os.wait4` itself.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/proc.py:_note_cost

chunk_findings.detail: The test runs `P.run_shell(f"{_PY} -c '{_BURN}' & wait")` and asserts the shell line’s resources show `cpu_user_s + cpu_sys_s >= 0.35`. On POSIX with a `shell=True`-style `run_shell`, the direct child is `/bin/sh -c "python ... & wait"`; that shell spends almost no CPU and the Python background child is a descendant, not the direct child. `wait4` on the shell returns only the shell’s own rusage, and putting the shell in its own process group does not make `wait4` aggregate descendants. The assertion will fail (or the capture would have to misreport the shell’s own usage as the child’s).
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_resource_capture.py::test_a_process_tree_is_attributed_to_the_shell_line

chunk_findings.detail: On macOS, `ru_inblock` and `ru_oublock` from `getrusage`/`wait4` are not implemented and are reported as 0 regardless of what the child did. This diff removes the platform check that previously turned those unavailable values into `None`, so on macOS every measured child now records `io_in_blocks=0` and `io_out_blocks=0` even though block IO was not actually measured. For example, `from_rusage(_ru(ru_inblock=0, ru_oublock=0), platform="darwin")` now returns `0, 0`, while the deleted test `test_macos_block_io_is_unknown_not_zero` expected `None, None`. A gate or metric that trusts `resources_source="wait4"` and checks block IO will treat an unmeasurable macOS probe as a confirmed zero, violating the stated conformance that a probe which could not run must be recorded unavailable, never zero.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/resources.py:from_rusage (around the new `int(ru.ru_inblock)` / `int(ru.ru_oublock)` lines)

chunk_findings.detail: `from_rusage` now always returns raw `ru_inblock`/`ru_oublock`. On Darwin those fields are not maintained and are 0 for every command, so the code records a false zero instead of unknown. Example: `R.from_rusage(_ru(ru_inblock=0, ru_oublock=0), platform="darwin")` now yields `io_in_blocks=0, io_out_blocks=0`; the previous guard and the deleted `test_macos_block_io_is_unknown_not_zero` protected against exactly this. This contradicts the change’s own conformance text that “a probe that could not run is recorded unavailable, never zero or passed.”
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/resources.py:from_rusage

A child that does no block I/O should record a legitimate `0`, not appear as “unknown”.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_resource_capture.py:test_macos_block_io_is_unknown_not_zero

chunk_findings.detail: The new `except subprocess.TimeoutExpired` path meters the timed-out capture with `R.measure(None, before)`, i.e. a process-wide `RUSAGE_CHILDREN` before/after delta, not the timed-out child's own `wait4` rusage. Because `RUSAGE_CHILDREN` accumulates every child reaped by the ddflow process, a concurrent reap is charged to this command: if thread A calls `capture([sys.executable, "-c", "import time; time.sleep(30)"], timeout=0.3)` and thread B starts and reaps a CPU-heavy child while A is waiting, A's returned `Resources.cpu_user_s` includes B's CPU although the sleep command used almost none. This is the previously confirmed capture-delta misattribution still present in the new timeout path.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/proc.py:capture timeout except

chunk_findings.detail: The burn fixture now allocates 200 MB (`bytearray(200 * 1024 * 1024)`) and the real-child tests require peak RSS of at least 180 MB, regressing the earlier reduction to 100 MB/90 MB. In a supported but memory-constrained CI environment (for example a 128 MB cgroup limit, or several pytest-xdist workers each trying to allocate 200 MB), the child raises `MemoryError`, so `P.run_shell(...).resources` is not usable and `test_a_real_child_that_allocates_and_burns_cpu_is_measured` plus the maxrss assertions in `test_each_command_gets_its_own_numbers_not_a_running_total` fail.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_resource_capture.py:_BURN

chunk_findings.detail: The claimed fix for the macOS block-I/O guard is not present: `io = (platform or sys.platform) != "darwin"` makes `from_rusage` discard `ru_inblock`/`ru_oublock` for every Darwin call. Given a Darwin rusage/fake with `ru_inblock=123` and `ru_oublock=456`, the function returns `(None, None)` instead of the reported integers, while the same rusage with `platform="linux"` returns `(123, 456)`. The new test only exercises zeros, so it locks in the platform guard and does not verify that nonzero block I/O is preserved. This reintroduces the previously accepted defect and contradicts the triage claim that the guard had been removed.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/resources.py:from_rusage

chunk_findings.detail: Darwin’s `struct rusage` exposes `ru_inblock` and `ru_oublock`, and the kernel reports block input/output counts, so this code discards a real available metric on a supported platform. The new test `test_macos_block_io_is_unknown_not_zero` locks in `(None, None)` for `platform="darwin"`, even though a child doing block I/O on macOS should report numeric values rather than `None`. This is the same defect as prior finding 11; the triage says the guard was removed, but the current diff re-adds it here.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/resources.py:from_rusage

chunk_findings.detail: `_BURN` still allocates `bytearray(150 * 1024 * 1024)` and the tests require `maxrss_kb >= 130 * 1024`. In a memory-constrained but supported CI environment with a 128 MiB cgroup, the child raises `MemoryError`, so `r.ok` is false and `test_a_real_child_that_allocates_and_burns_cpu_is_measured` and `test_each_command_gets_its_own_numbers_not_a_running_total` fail. Lowering from 200 MiB to 150 MiB does not answer the low-memory failure; the allocation is still not adaptive or skippable under a smaller limit.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_resource_capture.py:_BURN

chunk_findings.detail: This path records per-command cost from a `RUSAGE_CHILDREN` before/after delta. `ru_maxrss` is a high-water mark over all children already waited for, not a cumulative counter, so a before/after delta cannot recover the newly run child’s peak RSS. For example, if an earlier ddflow child peaked at 100 MB and then this capture path runs a child that peaks at 1 MB, the after snapshot still reports the prior 100 MB high-water mark; subtracting yields 0 KB (or reporting the after value yields 100 MB), so the evidence misreports `maxrss_kb` for a command that actually allocated memory. The delta source should mark peak RSS unavailable rather than emit a per-command `maxrss_kb` that is structurally wrong.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/proc.py:run_shell capture path (`resources=R.measure(None, before)`)

chunk_findings.detail: `p.communicate(timeout=wait)` is a standard Unix `subprocess.Popen` call: when it returns normally it has already called `Popen.wait()` and reaped the child. `_note_cost` is then called after that reap, so the kernel can no longer supply per-child `wait4` rusage for `p.pid`; an `os.wait4(p.pid, 0)` attempt after a normal `communicate()` return gets `ECHILD`. Thus, for a gate command that exits normally, the new code cannot produce the intended `resources_source="wait4"` per-command CPU/RSS/IO evidence. If `R.measure` falls back to a `RUSAGE_CHILDREN` delta, the values are approximate over every child reaped since `before` (for example the watcher or another concurrent child), not the gate command’s own usage. The rusage must be captured before the child is reaped, or stored by the code that reaps it, rather than after standard `communicate()` has already reaped it.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/proc.py:436 (`_note_cost` call after `p.communicate`)

chunk_findings.detail: The change introduces direct OS resource capture in `ddflow/infra/resources.py` and wires the concrete result object into `cmdrunner._finish` and `gates.runner._cost_evidence`, rather than exposing kernel child rusage/wait4 through a port in `ddflow/adapters`. Kernel rusage/wait4 is an external dependency outside the process (the guidance explicitly lists subprocess tools, clocks, and environment as things that must be ported), so any fake, swap, or unsupported-platform test has to reach into the concrete `infra.resources` module and shared service files instead of using a single adapter port; this violates [r-adapters].
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/resources.py (new) / ddflow/services/cmdrunner.py:185

chunk_findings.detail: This test runs `P.run_shell(f"{_PY} -c '{_BURN}' & wait")` and requires `cpu_user_s + cpu_sys_s >= 0.35`. On POSIX, the runner’s direct child is the shell; the Python process is a grandchild and is reaped by the shell’s `wait`. `wait4()` returns rusage only for the direct child being waited on, and `getrusage(RUSAGE_CHILDREN)` reports only direct children that the calling process has waited for. Starting the shell in a new process group does not make the runner the parent of the background Python process. Therefore on Linux/macOS the runner will normally see the shell’s tiny CPU time, not the Python burn’s ~0.4s, so the assertion fails unless tree attribution is done by some non-stdlib mechanism not described in the change.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_resource_capture.py:test_a_process_tree_is_attributed_to_the_shell_line

chunk_findings.detail: This test asserts that a successful `P.capture([sys.executable, "-c", "print(1)"])` reports `resources_source == "delta"`. The stated intent is that capture uses per-child `wait4` and falls back to a before/after `RUSAGE_CHILDREN` delta only when `wait4` is not usable. For the direct child in this test, `wait4` is usable on POSIX (the same `MeteredPopen`/`wait4` path used by `run_shell` can capture pipes). Thus the test either rejects a conforming `wait4` implementation or encodes that the shipped `capture` uses approximate deltas even when `wait4` is available, violating the “fallback only when wait4 is not usable” requirement.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_resource_capture.py:test_capture_reports_an_approximate_delta

chunk_findings.detail: `run_shell` passes a mutable `cost` list into `run(...)` and then derives `ShellResult.resources` from `cost[0]`, but the `run` implementation never mutates that list. The diff adds the `cost` parameter and a `before = R.children_snapshot()` call, then starts `MeteredPopen`, but adds no `R.measure(...)` result and no `cost.append(...)`/`cost[0] = ...` after the child is waited. As a result `cost` remains empty for success and timeout alike, so every command executed via `run_shell` returns `resources=None`. This defeats the intended wait4 resource capture for `run_shell`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/proc.py:416 (`run` / `run_shell` cost list)

chunk_findings.detail: The change adds a new external resource-measurement dependency under `ddflow/infra` and consumes it directly from `ddflow/infra/proc.py`. The project rule requires every external dependency to go through a port in `ddflow/adapters`, but no `ddflow/adapters` port is added in this manifest; the new `resources` module is not an adapter port. This violates [r-adapters] and prevents the single-place swap/fake that the rule calls for.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/proc.py:29 / ddflow/infra/resources.py [r-adapters]

chunk_findings.detail: After `p.communicate()` returns on the normal success path, the child process has already been reaped by `subprocess` (`communicate` calls `self.wait()` after reading EOF, so `p.returncode` is non-None). On Linux/macOS, `os.wait4(p.pid)` then raises `ChildProcessError` (ECHILD); there is no per-child rusage left to collect. Example: `run_shell(["sh","-c","python -c 'range(10**6)'"], cost=[])` — the command completes, `_note_cost(cost, p, before)` calls `R.measure` after the pid is gone, so the advertised wait4 per-child capture cannot happen; it either propagates the ECHILD error instead of returning a `CompletedProcess` or silently falls back to the approximate `RUSAGE_CHILDREN` delta, never recording the child's own cpu/maxrss/io. The call must happen before any `wait()`/`communicate()` reap, or the run loop must perform its own read/select loop and call `os.wait4` itself.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/proc.py:_note_cost

chunk_findings.detail: The test runs `P.run_shell(f"{_PY} -c '{_BURN}' & wait")` and asserts the shell line’s resources show `cpu_user_s + cpu_sys_s >= 0.35`. On POSIX with a `shell=True`-style `run_shell`, the direct child is `/bin/sh -c "python ... & wait"`; that shell spends almost no CPU and the Python background child is a descendant, not the direct child. `wait4` on the shell returns only the shell’s own rusage, and putting the shell in its own process group does not make `wait4` aggregate descendants. The assertion will fail (or the capture would have to misreport the shell’s own usage as the child’s).
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_resource_capture.py::test_a_process_tree_is_attributed_to_the_shell_line

chunk_findings.detail: On macOS, `ru_inblock` and `ru_oublock` from `getrusage`/`wait4` are not implemented and are reported as 0 regardless of what the child did. This diff removes the platform check that previously turned those unavailable values into `None`, so on macOS every measured child now records `io_in_blocks=0` and `io_out_blocks=0` even though block IO was not actually measured. For example, `from_rusage(_ru(ru_inblock=0, ru_oublock=0), platform="darwin")` now returns `0, 0`, while the deleted test `test_macos_block_io_is_unknown_not_zero` expected `None, None`. A gate or metric that trusts `resources_source="wait4"` and checks block IO will treat an unmeasurable macOS probe as a confirmed zero, violating the stated conformance that a probe which could not run must be recorded unavailable, never zero.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/resources.py:from_rusage (around the new `int(ru.ru_inblock)` / `int(ru.ru_oublock)` lines)

chunk_findings.detail: `from_rusage` now always returns raw `ru_inblock`/`ru_oublock`. On Darwin those fields are not maintained and are 0 for every command, so the code records a false zero instead of unknown. Example: `R.from_rusage(_ru(ru_inblock=0, ru_oublock=0), platform="darwin")` now yields `io_in_blocks=0, io_out_blocks=0`; the previous guard and the deleted `test_macos_block_io_is_unknown_not_zero` protected against exactly this. This contradicts the change’s own conformance text that “a probe that could not run is recorded unavailable, never zero or passed.”
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/resources.py:from_rusage
